title: NHS weight-loss medicines: who qualifies and what to ask
seo_title: NHS weight-loss medicines: eligibility and GP checklist
summary: Who may qualify for NHS weight-loss medicines, why access varies, and a practical checklist for asking your GP or local service about support.
body:
**You may be able to get weight-loss medicine through the NHS, but there is no single UK eligibility rule.** The medicine, reason for treatment, health conditions, BMI and local service all matter. Meeting a published BMI threshold does not confirm that a prescription is suitable or available.

The useful first step is to ask your GP practice or local weight-management service **which assessment route is available and what help you can get now**. You can ask for weight-management support even if you do not qualify for a particular injection. The [NHS explains the wider support options](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/overweight-and-obesity/), including programmes, medicines and specialist assessment.

*Information checked on 5 October 2026. This is an editorial explanation of official guidance, not an individual assessment or an independent clinical review.*

## Why three different eligibility answers can all appear online

A medicine's **licence** describes its authorised use. A **NICE recommendation** describes the circumstances in which NHS use is recommended. **Commissioning and local delivery** concern the funded service, assessment route and implementation timetable. These are separate questions.

For example, [NICE TA1026](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1026) recommends tirzepatide for weight management in adults with an initial BMI of at least 35 kg/m² and at least one weight-related condition, alongside dietary and activity support. Lower BMI thresholds, usually reduced by 2.5 kg/m², apply for specified ethnic backgrounds. England's primary-care rollout initially prioritises a narrower group.

That is why “NICE recommends it” and “your practice cannot currently offer it” can describe different parts of the pathway. Ask which rule is being applied, rather than assuming that one online calculator settles it.

## NHS weight-loss injections: the key distinctions

These are summaries of the **weight-management appraisals**, not a complete prescribing checklist or a promise of local availability.

| Medicine | Main distinction in NICE weight-management guidance |
|---|---|
| Tirzepatide, also called Mounjaro | TA1026: initial BMI at least 35 plus a weight-related condition; relevant ethnicity adjustments. England has phased primary-care access. |
| Semaglutide, also called Wegovy | TA875: a weight-related condition plus BMI at least 35, or BMI 30–34.9 with the specified specialist-referral criteria. Specialist provision and a maximum two-year course apply under this appraisal; relevant ethnicity adjustments apply. |
| Liraglutide, also called Saxenda | TA664: BMI at least 35, non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (raised blood sugar below the diabetes range) and high cardiovascular risk, through a specialist service; relevant lower BMI thresholds apply. |

Read the full [tirzepatide](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1026), [semaglutide](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta875) and [liraglutide](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta664) guidance for the conditions attached to each recommendation. These medicines are not the whole NHS pathway: [other options include orlistat and non-medicine support](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/overweight-and-obesity/).

**The reason for prescribing matters too.** Diabetes treatment has different criteria. There is also a separate [NICE semaglutide recommendation for cardiovascular risk reduction, TA1152](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1152), published in May 2026. Do not apply the TA875 weight-management restrictions to every possible semaglutide indication. Ask your clinician which guidance applies to your care.

## England: what the phased tirzepatide rollout means now

As checked on 5 October 2026, the published primary-care cohorts include:

| Access cohort | BMI before relevant ethnicity adjustment | Qualifying conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Cohort 1, introduced first | At least 40 | At least four of the five conditions below |
| Cohort 2, introduced from 23 June 2026 | 35–39.9 | At least four of the five conditions below |

The five conditions are type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnoea and dyslipidaemia (abnormal blood fats). The BMI adjustment is 2.5 kg/m² for people from South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean backgrounds. The service checks the applicable diagnostic definitions.

The [current NHS Cheshire and Merseyside patient guidance](https://cheshireandmerseyside.nhs.uk/your-health/prescribing/statements/mounjaro-tirzepatide/) sets out these cohorts and makes clear that practice participation and availability can vary. The [NHS England Digital cohort appendix](https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/data-collections-and-data-sets/data-collections/tirzepatide-in-primary-care-data-collection/prescribing-activity-of-tirzepatide-mounjaro-in-primary-care-settings/appendix) also distinguishes the rollout cohorts. Specialist-service access is a separate route; ask whether it applies to you.

Later expansion is planned, but a future cohort is not current eligibility. Check the [NHS England patient information](https://www.england.nhs.uk/ourwork/prevention/obesity/medicines-for-obesity/weight-management-injections/) and your local service when seeking an assessment.

## Your GP appointment checklist

You do not need to arrive knowing which medicine to request. Arrive ready to explain what is difficult and what you want help with.

**Prepare one short note:**

- Your recent weight history, if you have it. Bring accurate records rather than trying to adjust a number to fit an eligibility rule.
- Your diagnosed conditions, current medicines and supplements, and previous treatment or side effects.
- Support you have tried, what helped and what was difficult to maintain.
- The practical barriers: shifts, food costs, pain, low mood, family responsibilities or difficulty attending appointments.
- What better health would let you do: walk comfortably, manage work, sleep better or feel more confident.

A useful opening is: “I'd like help managing my weight. Can we review the support available and whether I need a specialist assessment?”

**Ask these five questions:**

1. Which weight-management service can assess me, and do I need a referral or can I refer myself?
2. If medicine is considered, which eligibility and local access rules apply now?
3. Who would prescribe and review it, and whom would I contact between appointments?
4. What dietary, activity or behavioural support comes with treatment, and what support can I get while waiting?
5. What happens if treatment is unsuitable, causes problems, does not help enough or ends?

Before leaving, ask for the next action, who is responsible and when to check back. “Wait for contact” is easier to manage when you know which service will contact you and how to follow up.

## Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland

England's cohort timetable is not a UK-wide rule.

- **Scotland:** use [NHS inform's weight-loss information](https://www.nhsinform.scot/healthy-living/weight-loss/) and ask your GP about your local health board's pathway.
- **Wales:** use [NHS 111 Wales information on obesity](https://111.wales.nhs.uk/Encyclopaedia/o/article/obesity/) and ask your GP or local health board which weight-management service is available.
- **Northern Ireland:** [nidirect's current weight-management services page](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/weight-management-services) explains developing services and local access. Ask your GP or Health and Social Care Trust about the appropriate route.

A medicine recommendation in another nation does not establish your local access.

## If the answer is “not currently available”

Ask what the reason is: clinical suitability, current rollout criteria, referral requirements or service availability. Then ask what support can be offered instead and whether circumstances that affect access will be reviewed.

The [NHS lists options for finding local support](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/overweight-and-obesity/), including checking your practice website and, in England, your Integrated Care Board website. Some programmes accept self-referrals. [NHS Better Health](https://www.nhs.uk/better-health/lose-weight/) also provides free resources.

Pick a manageable starting point, such as planning one regular meal, and discuss activity suited to your health. Avoid extreme restriction while waiting. If low mood, pain or eating difficulties are part of the problem, say so: support should take the whole situation into account.

Private treatment does not automatically transfer to the NHS. If you already have a prescriber, ask about transfer arrangements before ending that care and bring your treatment records.

## Common questions

### Can my GP prescribe a weight-loss injection?

Some tirzepatide weight-management prescribing is delivered through primary care in England. Your practice must confirm its arrangements and assess suitability. Other routes may involve specialist services.

### Is BMI 35 enough to qualify?

No. The medicine's recommendation, related conditions, treatment indication, relevant ethnicity adjustment and current service pathway all matter.

### Can I still ask for help if I do not qualify?

Yes. Ask about weight-management programmes, practical support and assessment of conditions that make weight difficult to manage. An injection threshold is not a threshold for deserving help.

For a broader explanation of routes, see our [NHS weight-loss medication pathways guide](/guides/nhs-weight-loss-medication-pathways). For your next appointment, use the checklist above and confirm one clear next step.

*Editorial update — 5 October 2026: the original publication date is retained. This revision clarifies current access cohorts, separates treatment indications and adds an appointment checklist and national information routes. It does not certify individual eligibility.*
